Actions represent everything a character can do in that span of time, and may be divided however the player wishes: move to an enemy, attack them, then pull away; attack twice in a row and activate a power or ability; use a gadget, attack, then move. Thanks to this flexibility, each Turn can be used in a tactical and creative way, promoting dynamic scenarios worthy of a comic book story.

docs.title: The Three-Action Economy
docs.text:
As explained earlier, during a Round, a character has access to 3 Actions. They may be used all at once during the Turn, or they may be reserved for Reactions, which are a specific type of Action that breaks Initiative order.

As a rule, Actions are not interchangeable between different Rounds; a character cannot, for example, “bring forward” their Actions from the next Round into the current one, gaining six Actions and then having none in the following Round. In addition, Actions not used by the end of that Round are lost.

docs.title: Reaction
docs.text: This is a specific type of Action performed in response to another, requiring a trigger, such as actively blocking a strike or getting out of the way of a shot. To use a Reaction, the character must have at least one Action remaining from their total that Round.

docs.title: Attack
docs.text:
Cost: 1 Action

An Attack action involves a direct blow, such as a punch, a shot, or a sword slash. When a Hero makes an Attack, they make an Attack Test against the target’s Defense value. If successful, they deal Damage directly to the target’s Resolve.

docs.title: Attack Test
docs.text: When making an Attack Test, always roll 1d20 + Accuracy + Attack Bonus to determine the result. In most cases, an Attack Test will always be compared to the target’s Defense.

docs.title: Melee Attack
docs.text: This is made using hands or melee weapons. It generally occurs when two opponents are at Adjacent distance.

docs.title: Ranged Attack
docs.text:
This type of attack involves projectiles such as bullets, arrows, blasts of fire, or laser beams. It is made against targets that are one or more distances away from a Hero. Depending on the Grade of the Power, the quality of the weapon, or the technology involved, an Attack may reach Close, Far, or even Distant targets.

Unless explicitly stated otherwise, Ranged Attacks suffer Disadvantage when made at Adjacent distance.

docs.title: Splash Page
docs.text: In an Attack, a Splash Page only occurs if the character exceeds the target’s Defense by 10 or more. When that happens, the number of dice rolled for Damage is doubled.

docs.title: Multiple Attacks
docs.text:
A character may use as many available Actions as they have to attack in a turn, but if they do, they risk lowering their combat accuracy. Each additional Attack beyond the first causes the character to suffer –5 (cumulative with each subsequent attack) on their Attack Tests until the beginning of their next turn. A character’s Attack count resets on their next turn, which means Attacks made as Reactions outside their Turn still count toward the total.

Penalty modifiers from different sources do not stack. If a character has one ability that changes the penalty to –2 instead of –5 and another that changes it to –3 instead of –5, the character uses whichever is more favorable.

Attack Penalty 2nd Attack –5 3rd Attack –10 4th Attack –15 5th Attack –20

docs.title: Activation
docs.text:
Cost: Variable

Activating a Power, Maneuver, Archetype Ability, and similar effects requires an Activation. As a rule, this requires 1 Action, but that number may vary as indicated in the description.

docs.title: Dodge
docs.text:
Cost: 1 Action (Reaction)

A Dodge occurs when a Hero quickly moves out of the way of an incoming attack. When that happens, the Hero’s Agility is added to their Defense until the end of the Turn.

docs.title: Block
docs.text:
Cost: 1 Action (Reaction)

A Block occurs when a Hero prepares to absorb the impact of an attack, increasing their Defenses. When a Hero uses Block, they add Resistance to their Defense against the next incoming Attack.

docs.title: Extend Range
docs.text:
Cost: 2 Actions

A Hero may take a deep breath and prepare to make a Ranged Attack with a weapon; the Hero may extend the range by 1 Distance, spending 2 Resolve.

docs.title: Disarm
docs.text:
Cost: 3 Actions

You may remove a weapon that the target is carrying. Make an Opposed Test against the target. If the action involves brutally tearing a sword from the target’s hands, use Potency; if you shoot the target directly in the hand so that they drop the pistol, use Accuracy. There are countless ways to disarm someone, and virtually any Attribute may be used in this situation. The target decides which Attribute they will use in the Opposed Test.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Cost: 1 Action + Movement Actions

Often on the battlefield, Heroes need to assist their allies. The Help action includes rescuing, moving someone out of the way, or even applying medical care to fallen allies. Help is an umbrella term that includes all of these possibilities.

docs.title: Move
docs.text:
Cost: 1 Action + Movement Actions

Sometimes an ally is unable to leave a dangerous place, such as the edge of a volcano about to erupt, and that is when you fly, run, or even pilot a vehicle toward them. You spend Movement Actions normally to reach your ally, and +1 Action to relocate them up to 1 Distance from your point of origin.

docs.title: Cover
docs.text:
Cost: 1 Action

You provide strategic cover for your ally, whether through a hail of bullets, a smoke bomb, or a powerful gust of wind. The next Attack against your ally suffers Disadvantage.

docs.title: Defend
docs.text:
Cost: 3 Actions

You strategically position yourself to defend an ally Adjacent to you, placing yourself between them and their attacker. Until the beginning of your next turn, Attacks made against that ally suffer Disadvantage, while Attacks made against you gain Advantage.

docs.title: THE DOOMSDAY CLOCK
docs.text:
In Rescue scenes, missions, or even long-term villainous plans, the Editor draws a circle and divides it into several parts: this is the Doomsday Clock. It is a tool that represents the progress and complexity of danger in a Rescue scene.

Each time the Heroes fail, the group takes too long to act, or an external force such as a villain or a catastrophe makes things worse, the Editor advances the clock as a way of showing that the danger is approaching and drastic consequences are near.

docs.title: Completing the Clock
docs.text: When completely filled, the clock triggers the worst possible scenario, and the Heroes fail. The civilians are not saved, the bomb explodes, and the catastrophe is not contained. Now the Heroes must deal with the consequences, such as public opinion, the weight of failure, and the villains completing their objectives.

docs.title: Four-Part Clock:
docs.text:
The Hospital Explosion

A four-part Clock represents moderate challenges, but ones that require coordination and teamwork to resolve.

A bomb has been planted in a downtown Hospital. They must act quickly before the worst happens!

docs.title: First Part Filled
docs.text: Panic sets in when the alarms sound, and the population rushes out in desperation.

docs.title: Second Part Filled
docs.text: Smoke and soot spread throughout the place, making action more difficult.

docs.title: Third Part Filled
docs.text:
Only a few minutes remain before the bomb explodes. The Heroes need to find it as fast as possible!

Henchmen appear to cause even more confusion.

docs.title: Fourth Part Filled
docs.text:
The Heroes fail to stop the explosion. Many civilians are injured and the hospital’s structure is damaged.

Each time a Hero fails a Heroic Action in Rescue scenes or during a mission, one part of the Clock is filled. When the Clock fills all its parts, the Heroes fail the Rescue, and the worst happens.

docs.title: HEROIC ACTIONS
docs.text: Like combat, Rescue Scenes are divided into Turns and Rounds. Heroic Actions are broad and varied, encompassing a different number of maneuvers and stunts a Hero can perform. On their Turn, a Hero can perform up to three Heroic Actions, and can choose how many of it they will use: the bigger the number of actions spent on a Heroic Action, the bigger are the chances of succeeding.

docs.title: Number of Actions
docs.text:
A Hero can choose to focus on several different tasks, such as rushing into a burning building to rescue falling civilians, putting out the flames, and still coordinating firefighters in a joint effort to contain the rest of the fire. This is entirely possible, but the more different tasks a Hero attempts to perform in this way, the more difficult their job becomes.

In JLU RPG, the more a Hero focuses on a single objective during a Rescue Scene, the better, after all, teams work together to cover as much ground as possible. For each Action a Hero spends focusing on the same Heroic Action, their chances of success increase.

1 Action: If a Hero uses one of their Actions to save the civilians from the burning building, they make the roll against the Tension established by the Editor normally.

2 Actions: If the Hero uses two of their three available Actions to save the civilians from the burning building, they gain Advantage on the Test.

3 Actions: If the Hero uses all three of their Actions to save the civilians from the burning building, no Test is required, and the Hero treats their result as a 20 for the purposes of the Test. However, if a result of 20 is still insufficient to meet the required Tension number, the action is considered a failure.

docs.title: Heroic Effort
docs.text: In a Rescue Scene, a Hero may go beyond their Limits, putting themselves at risk to save those in need. Heroic Effort allows the Hero to mark a Condition in order to receive an Extra Action on their Turn or recover an amount of Resolve equal to their Tier base.

docs.title: Remove Debris
docs.text: Buildings collapse, bridges fall. Situations like these require a Potency or Resistance Test against Tension. Failure: Lose 2 Resolve.

docs.title: Calm the Population
docs.text:
Panic is one of the great dangers in risky situations, and preventing the crowd from losing control is essential.

Test: Spirit vs. Tension

Failure: Mark the Stunned Status.

docs.title: Command the Crowd
docs.text:
Bringing a crowd to safety in an organized way is essential to ensure the success of a rescue and avoid harm.

Test: Mind vs. Tension

Failure: Mark one Condition.

docs.title: Save the Falling
docs.text:
The critical moment when civilians are falling from collapsing places or hanging from a precipice requires quick action.

Test: Agility vs. Tension

Failure: Lose 5 Resolve; if you have no Resolve, mark two Conditions.

docs.title: Contain Environmental Threat
docs.text:
A fire spreads, a chemical leak fills the air with toxic gases, or high-voltage cables come loose, threatening to electrocute everyone. The Hero must use their powers or quick thinking to isolate or neutralize the danger.

Test: Mind or Spirit vs. Tension Failure: The Hero is caught by the danger. Gain the “Engulfed” Status (burned, poisoned, etc.), and the Doomsday Clock advances one extra segment.

docs.title: Disarm Device
docs.text:
A time bomb is about to explode, a nuclear reactor is overloading, or an unstable portal threatens to suck in everything around it. Time is running out, and a steady hand or a brilliant mind is required.

Test: Mind or Accuracy vs. Tension Failure: The device becomes even more unstable. The Doomsday Clock advances two segments immediately.

docs.title: RECOVERY
docs.text: Heroic life takes its toll, and even the mightiest of Heroes still suffers harm after an intense mission or brutal combat. Even if you are made for action, recovery is still necessary.

docs.title: Recovering Resolve
docs.text:
Resolve is the resource Heroes will use most. Recovering it is simple: all spent Resolve is restored at the beginning of a new Scene, as long as the Hero pauses to clear their head, take a deep breath, and prepare for another challenge. In other words, Heroes need to go through an Interlude Moment to recover their Resolve points.

If an Interlude Moment turns into a Danger or Combat scene, at the Editor’s discretion, Heroes recover only half of their Resolve.

docs.title: Recovering Conditions
docs.text: Conditions do not recover as easily as Resolve. Of course, Scratched and Tired disappear at the end of a Scene, but the rest of the Conditions require the Heroes to recover in a more elaborate way. At least one Interlude Moment focused on healing is necessary, in which the Heroes withdraw to a safe place and recover their strength. Here, if the Interlude Moment is interrupted by some danger or villain, the Conditions remain.

docs.title: DEATH
docs.text:
It is already a well-worn comic-book cliché: no one really dies, and when it happens, they do not stay dead for long. Deaths in JLU RPG are rare, and even if a Hero is Defeated by a powerful enemy, they still live to see another day.

A Hero only dies if the player decides that this is the appropriate moment for their departure. Maybe it was while fighting a powerful enemy, sacrificing themselves to defeat evil, or they spent all their energy saving innocents from disaster and perished in the process. Sacrifice and altruism are intrinsic to Heroes, and the death of a character can provide continuity for many future Issues.

docs.title: ROLLING THE DICE
docs.text:
The core mechanic governing moments of uncertainty in JLU RPG is the roll of a twenty-sided die (d20). Whenever a Hero tries to perform an action whose result is uncertain, they must make a Test. The formula is simple:

Test Result = 1d20 + Relevant Attribute + Other Bonuses (Powers, abilities, equipment, etc.)

This result is then compared to a target number defined by the Editor, known as Tension. One important note for players: the player never asks for Tests; they always suggest a course of action, and the Editor decides the appropriate Test and Attributes.

docs.title: Advantage
docs.text: Certain abilities or favorable situations may grant Advantage to a character. When this happens, the player rolls two dice (d20 for Tests, or the Damage Die for attacks) and keeps the better result. If for some reason a Hero gains more than one Advantage, they do not increase the number of dice rolled, but instead gain a +2 bonus for each Advantage beyond the first. Advantage and Disadvantage cancel each other out.

docs.title: Disadvantage
docs.text: Similar to Advantage, there are some unfavorable situations that complicate a Hero’s life. When this happens, they suffer Disadvantage. The player rolls two dice and keeps the worse result.

docs.title: Increase by One Step
docs.text:
Some abilities allow you to increase your Tier Die by one step. When you do this, follow the order below. Increasing the Die beyond d12 means rolling a d12 with Advantage.

d6 → d8 → d12

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Justice League Unlimited is a game built around Actions: throughout the game, characters will perform many of them. Flying quickly to save endangered innocents, landing the final shot on the villain who’s terrorising the city, calming a riotous crowd, and many other efforts are all examples of Actions. Think of them as a small cause that generates a narrative effect in a game situation.

Actions are widely used in combat, rescue scenes, social interactions, and environmental challenges... the list is virtually endless. At all times during the game, Heroes (and villains) will be performing Actions.

docs.title: TENSION
docs.text: Tension is the Editor’s main tool for defining the difficulty of any situation in the game. It is a numerical value that represents the danger and complexity of a task. The final word on the value of Tension always belongs to the Editor, who may adjust it based on various narrative factors.

docs.title: DIFFICULTY LEVELS
docs.text:
In Justice League Unlimited RPG, the division by Tiers allows the game to cover a wide variety of challenges appropriate to the many power levels a comic-book story encompasses. While a group of Year One Heroes deals with the chaos of the streets during an alien invasion, the World’s Finest deals directly with the intergalactic conqueror. For this reason, the Difficulty Levels (Routine, Challenging, Difficult, Heroic, and Impossible) have values calculated to better suit each Tier.

Routine: A task that a Hero of the corresponding Tier should be able to accomplish with some ease, though failure is still possible. Tier D Example (Tension 12): Stop a gang of ordinary thieves from robbing an ATM.

Challenging: The standard for heroic life. It represents a task that requires effort and presents a real risk of complications. Tier C Example (Tension 17): Stop falling debris from hitting civilians on a busy street.

Difficult: A task that will likely require planning, teamwork, or intelligent use of powers. Failure here has serious consequences. Tier C Example (Tension 20): Put together the clues left by a serial killer like the Riddler.

Tension Tier D Tier C Routine 12 15 Challenging 15 18 Difficult 18 21 Heroic 21 25 Impossible 26+ 28+

docs.title: TESTS
docs.text:
A Test occurs whenever there is an uncertainty in the outcome of an Action, so the dice are rolled against the Tension set by the Editor to resolve the uncertainty.

Success!: When a Hero obtains a value equal to or greater than the Tension, they achieve a Success.

Critical Success: Splash Page!: You know that incredible comic-book scene drawn by the artist you love, in full double-spread style? Here it works the same way. When a Hero exceeds the Tension by 15 or more or rolls a natural 20 on the d20 (that is, the value 20 on the die, without any bonuses), a Splash Page occurs. This is an epic moment in which the best possible result happens.

Failure: When a Hero gets a result lower than the Tension, we have a failure. The Editor describes how, just as the speedster was about to catch the Villain, they escape at the last instant and the portal closes.

Critical Failure: Editorial Cut!: When a Hero fails by 15 or more below the Tension, or rolls a natural 1 on the d20, we have a Critical Failure. Not only does the Hero fail their Test, but the worst happens. The Editor narrates how this disaster unfolds: perhaps the attempt to hold the truck falling off the bridge did not go as expected and now the Amazon is being dragged down with it, in freefall! How will she get out of this?

Close Call!: When the Hero fails to reach the Tension, but chooses to spend Resolve, they may spend Resolve points to increase the Test result. The result increases by 1 for each Resolve point spent. Close Call! cannot be used on Editorial Cuts.

docs.title: OPPOSED TEST
docs.text: When two forces enter into direct conflict, such as a race around the globe between two speedsters, an arm-wrestling match between the strongest beings on Earth, or a chess game between a genius and a quantum supercomputer, an Opposed Test is made. In an Opposed Test, both sides make a Test using the relevant attribute. Whoever gets the higher result wins the contest. In case of a tie, a new Test must be made. Note that an Opposed Test is not made against Tension, but rather against another result, and therefore effects that use or depend on Tension cannot be used.

docs.title: COMBAT
docs.text: Sometimes heroic work involves getting into a fight, after all, there are enemies who will not be convinced by words alone. Combat in JLU RPG is designed to be fast, dynamic and cinematic, but with a touch of tactics. Using the 3 Actions mechanic, Heroes will devise strategies, apply unusual plans and kick the backsides of many evildoers.

docs.title: Initiative
docs.text:
When a conflict begins, all parties involved compare their Agility score to decide who acts first. The order of turns is determined from the highest to the lowest. In case of a tie, both parts involved must make an Agility Test, and the winner is placed immediately above the loser.

Increasing Initiative: A character can force their Limits to increase their place on the Initiative order: By each Resolve point spent, they receive +1 during the Initiative phase.

docs.title: Inspire
docs.text:
Activation: 1

Some Heroes have a natural aura of command, fulfilling those around them with hope and determination. With this action, a Hero can inspire allies, pushing them beyond their Limits. To use this Action, the Spirit of the Hero must be higher than the target’s Spirit score. A target can only be affected by one of Inspire’s effects at a time.

Once per round, choose one ally that can see or hear you, and make a Spirit Test against the Tension set by the Editor. On a Success, choose on of the following:

You’ve Got This!: The target receives Advantage on their next Heroic Action.

Don’t Give Up!: A target receives a bonus to their next Attack, Block or Dodge equal to your Spirit value, as long as they are facing a threat with a Tier Higher than theirs.

Heroes Never Quit!: You can spend 1 Resolve Point to grant a target 1 Resolve Point, up to a maximum number of Resolve Points per Scene equal to your Spirit score.

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text:
Activation: 1

With this action, a Hero can shout orders and commands to their allies and civilians,acting like a true oracle and granting them tactical advantages. To use this Action, the Mind Attribute of the Hero must be higher than the target’s Mind. A target can only be affected by one Tactics effect at a time.

Once per Round, Choose one ally that can hear you and make a Mind Test against the Tension set by the Editor, on a Success, choose one of the following:

On your left!!: The target’s next Dodge receives a bonus equal to your Mind.

Engage!: Before the beginning of a Combat, the Target’s Initiative is increased in a value equal to half your Mind.

Attack!: The target next Attack receives a bonus equal to your Mind, limited by your Tier,+3.

Hold the line!: The Target receives Damage Reduction equal to your half your Mind score against the next Attack that targets them.

Move! Move! Move!: The Target receives one extra Move action that must be used on their next Turn.

Focus!: The Target next Opposed Test to resist a harmful effect, such as a Status effect receives Advantage. Focus can be used as a Reaction.

Brace for Impact!: The target gains a bonus equal to half your Mind score on their next Block.

docs.title: Turn
docs.text: A Turn is the moment when a Hero must act. During a turn, the character has 3 Actions. When all actions have been used or the participant declares the Turn ended, the Turn ends.

docs.title: Round
docs.text:
When everyone involved in the conflict has resolved their turns, the Round ends. Then a new Round begins, following the same Initiative order.

These three steps represent the basic flow of combat, which repeats until the confrontation is over.

docs.title: Basic Combat Resources
docs.text: It is necessary to understand some of the resources a character has during combat: how Resolve is used, how Damage works, and the dynamics of Attack and Defense are fundamental to the progress of the game.

docs.title: Resolve
docs.text: Using this resource activates powers and other abilities, and it is also the first line against Damage. In terms common to other games, think of Resolve simultaneously as your “life” and your “mana,” but even so, if it runs out, a character may still keep going. It is the stamina that must be used strategically. When Resolve runs out, a Hero must mark a Condition. (See Conditions later in this section.)

docs.title: Attack
docs.text: These are blows, shots, cuts and everything else. To make an Attack, roll 1d20 + Accuracy and compare it to the target’s Defense. If the result is higher, the Attack is successful. See more about Attack under Combat Actions.

docs.title: Defense
docs.text:
Defense is a character’s protection and their ability to avoid being hit. Do not think of it only as how tough a Hero’s skin or suit is; imagine it as the protective aura formed around them. A street thug would have a harder time keeping themselves from shaking long enough to shoot Batman than they would if they were shooting at a rookie vigilante.

Tier Defense Value E 12 D 15 C 18

Defense Value: A Hero’s Defense is equal to the base value provided by their Tier.

docs.title: Using Defense
docs.text: In combat, Defense is used when you are the target of an Attack, serving as the basic value the attacker needs to reach in order to hit you. Some attributes may be added to the base Defense value, increasing it against incoming attacks: Agility, Resistance, Spirit, and Mind may be used as protection against many different types of effects.

docs.title: Active Defense
docs.text: A Hero worth the name should always be ready to react to anything that is thrown, fired, struck or cast in their direction; that is where Active Defense comes in. With it, it is possible to add one of your Attributes to your Base Defense.

docs.title: Active Defense
docs.text:
Activation: Reaction

When using Active Defense, you prepare to receive an Attack. Choose one of the effects below and gain its effects until the end of the next Attack Action that targets you. A character may only have one Active Defense at a time. This Defense may be deactivated as a free action.

Dodge: A Dodge is made to get out of the way of an Attack, adding Agility to the Defense value.

Block: A Block uses Resistance to withstand the impact of blows that cause physical damage, adding Resistance to Defense.

docs.title: Damage
docs.text: Damage represents the harm and destruction a character causes (and suffers) during combat. Whenever an Attack hits, it deals Damage directly to the target’s Resolve. As a rule, a character’s basic Damage is equal to their Tier Damage Die + the indicated Attribute.

docs.title: Types of Damage
docs.text:
The game separates different types of Damage into four categories, which interact in different ways with Powers, abilities and other effects during combat: Physical, Energy, Magical, and Psychic.

These categories act as umbrellas, encompassing many different kinds of attacks under one label. Even so, one ability or another may not fit entirely into any of them; in that case, the Editor has the final word.

Physical: The most common type of Damage, caused by blows, melee weapons and projectiles. This type of Damage is normally associated with Potency.

Energy: Energy Damage includes pure energy sources or forces of nature, such as elements, energy blasts, light and shadows. This type of Damage is normally associated with Potency or Spirit.

Magical: This type of Damage comes from magical sources, such as spells or artifacts. Magical damage uses Spirit as its Attribute.

Psychic: Psychic Damage comes from sources that use mental power, such as telekinesis, telepathy, and illusion manipulation. The Attribute associated with this type of Damage is Mind.

docs.title: CONDITIONS
docs.text: Conditions are hazardous states that can be applied to Heroes over the course of a game. Conditions begin at “Scratched” and end at “Defeated.” Each time a Hero marks a Condition, they get closer and closer to defeat.

docs.title: Marking Conditions
docs.text:
Generally, Conditions are marked when receiving a significant amount of Damage: perhaps that energy blast broke your spirit, or that cross punch knocked the breath out of you. There are some ways to mark Conditions:

Choosing to Mark Them: When a character receives at least 10 points of Damage, they may mark a Condition, keeping their Resolve intact but absorbing the Damage directly. Even so, all excess damage beyond the 10 points negated in favour of marking a condition is still deducted from the Hero’s Resolve.

Example: If a Hero receives 13 points of Damage from a Villain, they may mark one Condition to take only 3 points to their Resolve. In another situation, that same Hero receives 20 points of Damage, but this time they choose to mark two Conditions, absorbing 10 points of Damage with each one. Since there is no excess Damage, their Resolve remains intact.

docs.title: Condition Track
docs.text:
Conditions follow an order and are not marked at random. In ascending order, they are: Tired, Scratched, Injured, Wounded, and Defeated. A character cannot mark the “Scratched” Condition without first having marked “Tired,” and so on. Some Powers grant extra Conditions, which must be counted before Scratched, while preserving the order of the track.

Tired: The fight is dragging on, you begin to pant.

Scratched: It was just a little scratch. There’s still plenty of firewood left to burn. Apply –2 to all d20 rolls.

Injured: That one hurt. Not enough to stop you, but it hurt. Apply –4 to all your d20 rolls.

Wounded: It is time to start worrying. Characters who are Wounded suffer Disadvantage to all their d20 rolls.

Defeated: The Hero is out of combat and at the Editor’s mercy. Their fate will be decided by the course of the story.

docs.title: Fighting Without Resolve
docs.text:
When Resolve is depleted, a character becomes Vulnerable: if they suffer 1 point or more of Damage, they must mark one Condition. In addition, for each multiple of ten taken while Vulnerable, mark one additional Condition.

When in doubt, follow the table:

Amount of Damage Conditions Marked 1–10 1 11–20 2 21–30 3 31–40 4 41+ Defeated

Example: Nightwing is out of Resolve points, which means he becomes Vulnerable. The Metal Sentinel he and the Titans are fighting lands a powerful strike, dealing 5 points of damage. Nightwing marks one Condition box. That one hurt!

docs.title: KNOWLEDGE
docs.text: A Hero without Knowledge on a particular subject is UNABLE to make any Test on that subject. Without the Piloting Knowledge, your Hero may be able to drive a car, but will not be able to perform maneuvers or chases, for example, because those would involve Tests.

docs.title: Acquiring Knowledge
docs.text: Each Knowledge costs 4 PAX, and grants all the abilities listed in that field. Possessing a Knowledge is enough for a Hero to be a considerable force in that area, a true expert.

docs.title: Acrobatics
docs.text:
You practically fly through the city. Leaping over buildings, climbing walls, and performing incredibly agile maneuvers are part of your everyday life.

Climbing: When climbing any surface, leaping over buildings, or moving acrobatically, you gain Advantage on your Test.

Acrobatic Jump: Once per Issue, you gain an automatic success when performing an unbelievable feat of jumping or aerial movement.

Free Running: When you need to cross an area with obstacles (rooftops, walls, gaps), reduce the Tension by 5 to reach your destination quickly.

docs.title: Subterfuge
docs.text:
Going unnoticed, opening locks, and avoiding direct confrontation. Subterfuge is the art of not being seen and always having an ace up your sleeve.

Slip By: When making Agility Tests to sneak around, you gain Advantage.

Escapist: No bond can hold you. Once per Issue, if you are imprisoned or handcuffed, you may escape automatically.

Unaware Strike: Once per Scene, when dealing damage to a target that is unaware of your presence, you roll 1 additional Tier Damage Die.

docs.title: Tech
docs.text:
You are an expert in electronics, programming and advanced devices. You know how to hack, repair, and create last-minute gadgets.

Hacker: If you have the appropriate tools, you may break into sophisticated systems. You gain Advantage on Tests involving hacking systems and breaking codes.

Tech Rat: When you spend a Scene observing and studying a technological item, you completely understand how it works.

Technological Gadget: You carry a special gadget. At the beginning of the Issue, choose one Gear item from the list to receive. It must be used by the end of the Issue.

docs.title: Strategy
docs.text:
You are a master of tactics and planning. You can foresee movements, elaborate maneuvers and wild plans like no one else.

Plan B: You always have a backup plan. Once per Issue, when you fail a Test, you may describe how you had a plan up your sleeve and reroll the Test, keeping the second result.

Maneuver Number 7!: You prepared for this moment. At the beginning of a Scene, choose one Attribute on a single target character. They receive a bonus equal to your Tier on their next roll with that Attribute.

Tactical Analysis: Once per Issue, you may quickly analyze your target. You must choose one of the following factors about the target to discover: a Weakness, their Resolve Points, one Attribute of your choice, or the first action they will take on their turn.

docs.title: LIMITATIONS
docs.text:
Every Hero worth the name has a weakness, after all, no one is completely invincible. Acting both as a mechanical weakness and a narrative hook, a Limitation is something that makes our Heroes tangible.

Think of the Martian Manhunter’s aversion to fire, Superman’s vulnerability to Kryptonite or Batman’s moral code. When choosing a Limitation, do not think that you are weakening your Hero: it is a chance to make the story more interesting.

docs.title: Choosing Limitations
docs.text:
As a rule, every Archetype offers one Limitation, such as the Enraged’s Side Effect. But beyond that, every player (with the exception of some Origins) must choose one more Limitation for their Hero.

Whenever your Hero is exposed to that Limitation in a narratively important moment, they will suffer a consequence. The Editor is the final arbiter of when a Limitation is activated, but players are encouraged to roleplay their own weaknesses and bring them into the story.

docs.title: Consequences of Limitations
docs.text:
Limitations manifest mechanically in several ways. As a rule, Limitations take precedence over other abilities or powers in the game: a Martian with Vulnerability to fire does not get rid of that Limitation if they acquire the Invulnerability Power to that element. Each type of consequence offers a different challenge:

Vulnerability: Applies the Vulnerable status when in contact with the target.

Example: A Hero of divine origin may have Vulnerability to profane or hell-forged weapons.

Weakness: You receive a negative Status when exposed to a certain condition.

Example: A Hero with Pyrophobia (fear of fire) may receive the “Frightened” Status whenever confronted with a large source of flames, suffering penalties on their actions.

Nullification: Your powers are temporarily turned off.

Example: A technological Hero may have their Exoskeleton power Nullified by an EMP.

Debilitation: You move up one level on your Condition track.

Example: A Hero whose physiology depends on darkness may suffer a Debilitation when exposed to direct sunlight, immediately marking the “Tired” Condition.

Impossibility: You are unable to use certain Knowledge or Traits in specific situations.

Example: A character with a rigid Code of Conduct against lying suffers Impossibility when trying to use any social Test to deceive someone.

docs.title: TRAITS
docs.text:
Think of Traits as the answers to important questions about your character that are not covered by Powers or Knowledge:

  • What do you have? (Resources, a secret base, a special vehicle)

  • Who do you know? (Contacts, allies, affiliation with an organization)

  • Who are you? (A reputation, striking beauty, a well-kept secret identity)

  • What can you do exceptionally well? (An innate talent beyond normal training)

In this quickstart, we provide Simple Traits, which cost 4 PAX each.

docs.title: Striking Appearance
docs.text: Your appearance is extraordinary, almost hypnotic. Once per Scene, when making a social test based on persuasion or seduction, you may spend 2 Resolve and automatically succeed.

docs.title: Polyglot
docs.text: You read, write, and speak all common human languages. In addition, your ease is so great that you may learn new languages simply by observing them for at least one Scene.

docs.title: Reliable Contact
docs.text: You have a guaranteed source of information (reporter, scientist, hacker, etc.). Once per Issue, you can ask the Editor to provide you with a useful clue from your Reliable Contact with relation to an investigation or mystery.

docs.title: Tough as Nails
docs.text: You are hard to bring down. Gain Damage Reduction 2, and when you mark the Defeated Condition, you may still act for one more Turn before falling.

docs.title: Catchphrase
docs.text:
Define a Catchphrase together with the Editor. Once per Scene, when you shout it loud and clear, choose one of the benefits below:

  • Reduce the Resolve cost of an ability by a value equal to your Tier.

  • Gain Advantage on your next roll.

docs.title: Pocket Gadgets
docs.text: You always have the right item ready for every situation. Once per Scene, you may spend 1 Resolve to receive one Gear item from the list.

docs.title: Voice of the Crowd
docs.text: In times of crisis, your voice stands out. When you choose this Trait, you receive Advantage on tests involving giving instructions, controlling, and calming crowds in Rescue Scenes.

docs.title: Influencer
docs.text:
You have many followers on social media. Maybe you have a channel where you post your patrols, a page where you review the latest heroic products or simply a fan page for your pet.

‘’Today’s sponsor is…’’ : Once per Issue, you may receive a Freebie, which is a small item such as a top-of-the-Line cellphone, a small weapon or an item of clothing.

docs.title: Secret Identity
docs.text:
You keep your civilian persona well protected and separate from your heroic life, whether through a mask or hypnotic glasses. No one (or almost no one) knows your identity. You gain Advantage on tests involving your civilian life, such as talking about the weather, standing in line, or taking the bus.

Put on the Glasses: Once per Issue, when you are engaged in some heroic activity, you may activate your civilian persona to leave the Scene quickly. When you do, you may reappear in an Adjacent Zone.

docs.title: Dynamic Duo
docs.text:
You have forged a powerful and genuine bond with another Hero. This Trait only functions if both Heroes involved possess it, and the Dynamic Duo only functions between the two of you. Whenever you are in the same Scene, both of you receive +1 Resolve, Accuracy, and Defense. In addition, whenever the Hero to whom you are linked suffers any amount of Damage, you receive 1 point of Damage.

Synchronized Attack: Once per Issue, the Dynamic Duo may make a powerful joint strike. For this Attack, both make separate Attack rolls, keeping the best result. Take each Hero’s Attribute that they used for the Attack, add them together, and divide the total by 2. The result (rounded down) is the Damage Bonus for the Attack.

docs.title: Affiliation
docs.text:
You are a member of an organization such as the Bat-Family or Steelworks. When using the fame of your affiliation in social Tests, you may spend 2 Resolve to gain Advantage on that Test.

Aid from the Group: Once per Issue, you may call for aid, such as receiving a technological device from Steelworks or access to Gotham’s most exclusive clubs through the Bat-Family.
